units.text: Method : name the cut, then work inside it. A complaint that mixes "this vowel is ugly" [phonetics/aesthetics] with "this sentence is ungrammatical" [syntax] with "that was rude" [pragmatics] is three jobs.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics

units.text: Phonetics describes how sounds are made (articulatory), how they travel (acoustic), and how they are heard (auditory).
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonetics

units.text: • pulmonic air from the lungs is the usual power source. • place of constriction: lips, teeth, alveolar ridge, palate, velum, glottis, ... • manner: stop, fricative, affricate, nasal, approximant, lateral, ... • voicing: vocal folds vibrating or not. • vowels: tongue height, backness, lip rounding; monophthong vs diphthong.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonetics

units.text: IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet) is the shared notation. The chart is owned by the International Phonetic Association. Fetch the chart. Do not invent a symbol. Do not guess a Unicode code point for a symbol — fetch Unicode / the IPA's own chart notes.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonetics

units.text: Narrow transcription tries to catch extra detail. broad transcription catches contrasts that matter for the language (and then you are already leaning on phonology).
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonetics

units.text: Check: you can point at a place and a manner, or you fetched a spectrogram / IPA cell. "it sounds like X" is a start, not a description.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonetics

units.text: Phonology is the system of contrasts and patterns in one language (or one variety).
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonology

units.text: Phoneme: a contrast that can distinguish words. allophone: a variant of a phoneme that does not, in that language, make a different word. A pair of words that differ by one contrast is a minimal pair. If you cannot exhibit a pair, you do not yet have a phoneme; you have a guess.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonology

units.text: Phonotactics: what sequences the language allows. English allows str- at the start of a word; Japanese (as usually described) does not allow the same cluster. Do not universalize English clusters.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonology

units.text: Prosody: stress, length, tone, intonation — sound structure above the segment. A tone language uses pitch to distinguish words. English uses pitch more for phrase meaning (intonation) than for word identity. Fetch the language before you declare it "tonal."
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonology

units.text: Check: contrast shown, or distribution stated, for this language. A phonetic difference is not automatically a phoneme.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › phonology

units.text: Morphology is how words are built from smaller meaningful pieces.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › morphology

units.text: Morpheme: a smallest conventional pairing of form and meaning (or grammatical job). free morphemes can stand as words. bound morphemes cannot (-ed, un-, case suffixes, ...).
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › morphology

units.text: Root vs affix. prefix, suffix, infix, circumfix as position names. stem is what the affix attaches to this round.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › morphology

units.text: Inflection fits a word to syntax (tense, number, case, agreement) without making a new dictionary word. derivation makes a new word (happy → happiness). compounding joins words (blackboard). The border is messy; name the job, not the trophy.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › morphology

units.text: Allomorphy: one morpheme, more than one shape (a / an; English plural -s / -z / -əz as a school example — fetch a phonology note if the exact conditioning is the job).
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › morphology

units.text: Productivity: whether speakers still make new forms with that pattern. A fossil is not a rule.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › morphology

units.text: Isolating / agglutinating / fusional / polysynthetic are tendencies, not boxes you drop a language into once. A language can be isolating in one corner and fusional in another.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › morphology

units.text: Check: can you split the word into pieces that each have a job? if a split explains nothing, do not split.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › morphology

units.text: Syntax is how words form phrases and clauses.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › syntax

units.text: Constituent: a group that behaves as a unit (moves together, replaces together, stands as an answer). Tests: substitution, movement, coordination, standalone answer. One test is weak; several agreeing is better.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › syntax

units.text: Head: the word that determines the phrase's kind. A noun phrase is headed by a noun (or a thing doing that job). A verb phrase by a verb. complement is required by the head. adjunct is extra (time, place, manner).
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › syntax

units.text: Argument structure: how many and what kind of arguments a verb wants (intransitive, transitive, ditransitive as school names). valency is the count. Languages mark this with order, case, agreement, or a mix.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › syntax

units.text: Word order as a default, not a law of nature. School labels SVO, SOV, VSO, ... describe a dominant order of subject, object, verb. English is typically SVO in declarative clauses. Japanese is typically SOV. Fetch the language. Do not call a focused or question order "the language's order."
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › syntax

units.text: Recursion / embedding: clauses inside clauses. "the cat the dog chased ran" is English syntax working, not a riddle from space.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › syntax

units.text: Ungrammatical means the system of that variety does not allow the form. It does not mean "I dislike it" or "a teacher marked it." mark the variety.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › syntax

units.text: Check: name the head, the clause type, and the test that shows a constituent. Vibe is not a tree.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › syntax

units.text: Semantics is conventional meaning: what the form contributes across situations, before this room and this feud.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › semantics

units.text: Sense vs reference (Frege's school cut): sense is the way of presenting; reference is what is picked out. "the morning star" and "the evening star" can share a reference and differ in sense. Philosophy pack owns the fight about propositions; this chapter owns the linguistic cut.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › semantics

units.text: Lexical semantics: word meaning, relations among words.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › semantics

units.text: • synonymy is rare if you demand identity of sense, register, and collocation. • antonymy has kinds (gradable hot/cold, complementary dead/alive, converse buy/sell). • hyponymy: spaniel is a hyponym of dog. • meronymy: part-whole (finger–hand). • homonymy vs polysemy: accident of form vs related senses of one word. Dictionaries disagree; fetch two and say so.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › semantics

units.text: Compositionality: the meaning of a complex form is computed from the meanings of the parts and the way they are combined. Idioms (kick the bucket) are the named exception: the whole is not the sum. Do not use the exception to deny the rule.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › semantics

units.text: Truth-conditional talk: a sentence's semantics as the conditions under which it would be true. Useful. Not the whole of meaning (ch 2.6).
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › semantics

units.text: Scope: which operator a word sits under. every student read a book has two school readings (one book vs possibly different books). If a fight is about "what it means," draw the scopes before you moralize.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › semantics

units.text: Check: paraphrase without upgrading. If you added a moral, that was not the semantics.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › semantics

units.text: Pragmatics is meaning that depends on this situation: who is speaking, to whom, with what shared knowledge, doing what action.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › pragmatics

units.text: Speech act: a sentence can assert, ask, order, promise, warn, name. The grammatical mood (declarative, interrogative, imperative) is a clue, not a census. "can you pass the salt?" is usually a request, not a question about ability.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › pragmatics

units.text: what is suggested without being said. some of the students passed often implicates not all. The implicature can be cancelled: some — in fact all — passed. Conventional meaning cannot be cancelled that way.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › pragmatics

units.text: Presupposition: what is taken as already on the table. the king of France is bald presupposes there is a king of France. A the-phrase often carries existence; fetch a semantics text if the job is the formal account.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › pragmatics

units.text: Deixis: meaning that needs the situation to lock: I, you, here, now, this. A transcript without the pointing is incomplete.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › pragmatics

units.text: Politeness and face are pragmatic. So is irony. So is register. None of these is "not grammar." they are grammar's neighbor.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › pragmatics

units.text: Check: what is said vs what is done vs what is hinted. If you cannot split those, you are not done.
units.section: The Structural Levels of Linguistics: From Acoustics to Pragmatics › pragmatics

units.text: is: The form you can hear, see, or feel (a stretch of sound, a written word, a sign-language form)
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.text: is: The concept that form is paired with in the system
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.topic: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign
units.text: The sign is both sides together. A sound with no conventional pairing is noise. A concept with no form in the language is not a word of that language.
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.topic: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign
units.text: Arbitrariness: the pairing is conventional, not a picture of the world. Nothing about the sounds of tree (English) or arbre (French) or ki (Japanese) is the tree. onomatopoeia and ideophones are limited iconic corners. They do not cancel the rule.
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.topic: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign
units.text: Value in the system: a sign means what it means against the other signs. A color word's range depends on how many color words the language cuts. This is not "language determines thought" as a slogan. It is: do not assume English cuts are nature.
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.topic: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign
units.text: Langue vs parole (Saussure's names): the shared system vs this utterance. synchrony vs diachrony: the system at a time vs the system through time. You can study today's grammar without telling the etymology. You can study the etymology without pretending it rules today's meaning (ch 8).
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.topic: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign
units.text: This is a teaching idea. Saussure's Cours de linguistique générale (1916) was assembled after his death from notes. It is a historical book, not a living standards body. There is no official Saussure site to fetch as primary authority. For philosophy of the cut, fetch Stanford Encyclopedia philosophy of linguistics. For the text, fetch a named edition from a library. Do not invent a homepage.
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.topic: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign
units.text: Later structuralists and then generativists (ch 11) argued with this picture. You do not need to pick a church to use the two-sided sign as a tool: form and meaning are paired; neither side is the whole word.
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.topic: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign
units.text: Check: can you name the form and the concept separately, then the pairing? if you only have a translation into English, you do not yet have the sign.
units.section: Semiotics: Signifier, Signified, and the Arbitrariness of the Sign

units.topic: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription
units.text: Writing records language with visible (or tactile) marks. It is not speech slowed down. It is a second system, with its own history, gaps, and politics.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription

units.text: Types are how the marks relate to the language, not how pretty they look.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: typical job of a graph: Consonants and vowels as letters; school examples (names, not a census): Latin, Greek, Cyrillic
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: typical job of a graph: Consonants; vowels optional or diacritic; school examples (names, not a census): Arabic, Hebrew (as usually described)
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: typical job of a graph: Consonant+vowel units; vowel changes by mark; school examples (names, not a census): Devanagari, Ethiopic
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: typical job of a graph: Syllables; school examples (names, not a census): Kana, Cherokee
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: typical job of a graph: Morphemes or words, often with phonetic parts; school examples (names, not a census): Chinese characters as usually taught
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: typical job of a graph: Graphs built from phonetic features; school examples (names, not a census): Hangul (as a design)
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: A real orthography is often a mix. English is an alphabet with heavy historical spelling. Japanese mixes morphographic kanji with syllabic kana. Do not force a type on a mixed page.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: Orthography is the conventional spelling of a language (or a standard of it). script is the set of graphs (Latin script, Arabic script). One script, many orthographies. One language, sometimes more than one script.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: Transliteration maps one script to another by letters. transcription maps sounds (often IPA). They are not the same job. Pinyin is a transcription/romanization of Mandarin, not "how Chinese is written" as a replacement for characters.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › kinds (school types)

units.text: Directionality: left-to-right, right-to-left, top-to-bottom, and historical boustrophedon. Unicode stores characters in logical order (roughly the order they are typed / the order of the language's stream), not necessarily the order of pixels. Bidirectional display is a rendering job. Fetch Unicode / W3C if the pixels fight the bytes.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › direction, space, punctuation

units.text: Word spacing is not universal. Many scripts historically did not put spaces between words. Punctuation sets are historical, not natural law. A full stop is a writing convention, not a clause detector you can trust in every language.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › direction, space, punctuation

units.text: Capitalization, hyphenation, and "a word" are orthographic decisions. Unicode encodes characters. It does not tell you where English hyphenates. Language-specific rules live in CLDR, layout notes (W3C language enablement), and dictionaries — fetch them.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › direction, space, punctuation

units.text: Writing underrepresents speech (no full intonation, often no exact vowel quality) and overrepresents history (English knight, French silent letters). spelling pronunciation is speech changing to match writing. eye dialect is writing pretending to be speech.
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › speech and writing come apart

units.text: Literacy is skill in a writing system. It is not intelligence and it is not "having a language."
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › speech and writing come apart

units.text: Check: script, orthography, direction. Speech or writing. If you cite a "letter," is it a graph, a phoneme, or a Unicode character? those three are different (ch 5).
units.section: Writing Systems: The Typology of Graphic Inscription › speech and writing come apart

units.topic: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings
units.text: This chapter is load-bearing. Numbers, ranges, and byte sequences below are from the Unicode Consortium's own pages and from RFC 3629 (UTF-8). If you need a specific character, fetch Unicode charts or Where is my Character? do not invent a code point from memory. Do not finish a U+.... from vibe.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings

units.text: The Unicode Standard is the universal character encoding for computer processing of text. Versions of Unicode are kept in sync with ISO/IEC 10646 (the Universal Character Set). A conformant Unicode implementation is also conformant to ISO/IEC 10646 on the shared repertoire.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is

units.text: Unicode assigns each character a unique numeric value (a code point) and a unique name. When written in text, a code point is hexadecimal after the prefix U+.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is

units.text: From Unicode's own technical introduction (fetched): U+0041 is LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A. That is an official example. For any other character you care about, fetch the chart.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is

units.text: Unicode encodes characters, not glyphs. A character is an abstract identity ("LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A"). A glyph is a mark on screen or paper. Fonts and rendering engines choose the glyph. Unicode does not specify size, serif, or handwriting.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is

units.text: Unicode encodes plain text. It does not encode bold, font, or "this is English." language identity is a separate tag (ch 12).
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is

units.text: Unicode's own list of fundamental principles (technical introduction): universal repertoire, logical order, efficiency, unification, characters not glyphs, dynamic composition, semantics, stability, plain text, convertibility.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › principles (names)

units.text: Unification: equivalent forms inside a script are not given duplicate codes just because two languages use them. CJK ideographs that are historically the same character are unified rather than triplicated per language. This is an encoding policy. It is not a claim that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are one language.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › principles (names)

units.text: Stability: assignment is additive. Characters are not removed or reinterpreted incompatibly. Fetch the Unicode stability policies if a product depends on that guarantee.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › principles (names)

units.text: Characters, not glyphs; dynamic composition: a base character plus combining marks can make what a reader thinks of as "one letter." a precomposed character (compatibility with older sets) can often be decomposed. "the same thing to a reader" can therefore be more than one code-point sequence. That fact is a security and matching issue (RFC 3629 section 10; Unicode Normalization). Fetch UAX #15 if you must compare strings for identity.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › principles (names)

units.text: Unicode is not "16-bit." Unicode's own FAQ: from Unicode 2.0 (July 1996) the encoded range is U+0000 .. U+10FFFF, a 21-bit codespace.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › codespace, not a 16-bit set

units.text: That range is the UTF-16 accessible range. Unicode and ISO 10646 policy: future assignments stay inside the integers UTF-16 can express. Over a million possible codes is a ceiling for characters, not for every ink mark in history.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › codespace, not a 16-bit set

units.text: The first 64K code points are the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP). Other planes are supplementary. Popular emoji, many historic scripts, and various CJK extensions live outside the BMP. "BMP-only" software is incomplete. Fetch the charts; do not assume a plane from a vibe.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › codespace, not a 16-bit set

units.text: Surrogate code points are reserved for UTF-16 pairing. They do not represent characters by themselves. RFC 3629: UTF-8 must not encode U+D800 .. U+DFFF as if they were characters.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › codespace, not a 16-bit set

units.text: Private-use code points have no universal meaning. Vendors may assign them. They are not portable identity. Do not cite a private-use code as "the Unicode for X."
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › codespace, not a 16-bit set

units.text: Unassigned code points are not yours to fill. Conformance: do not use unassigned codes; do not corrupt unknown characters.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › codespace, not a 16-bit set

units.text: For how many characters are encoded today, fetch the latest Unicode version. The technical introduction's running prose will lag. A count in this book would rot.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › codespace, not a 16-bit set

units.text: An encoding form maps code points to code units in bits.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › encoding forms: UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32

units.text: code unit: 8-bit bytes, 1-4 per character; school use: Web, files, most internet protocols
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › encoding forms: UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32

units.text: code unit: 16-bit units; supplementary characters as a surrogate pair; school use: Java, Windows APIs as commonly described
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › encoding forms: UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32

units.text: code unit: One 32-bit unit per code point; school use: Some Unix internals, easy indexing by code point
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › encoding forms: UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32

units.text: W3C internationalization : use UTF-8 for web content unless you have a special reason not to.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › encoding forms: UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32

units.text: A UTF (Unicode Transformation Format) is an algorithmic mapping from every Unicode code point except surrogate code points to a unique byte sequence. Round-trip is lossless. Reserved and unassigned code points still have mappings; that is required for round-trip.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › encoding forms: UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32

units.text: UCS-2 is obsolete terminology (Unicode FAQ): Unicode 1.1-era 16-bit, no supplementary characters. Do not say UCS-2 when you mean UTF-16.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › encoding forms: UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32

units.text: UTF-8 is the byte-oriented encoding form. Authoritative definition: the Unicode Standard (encoding forms). Internet profile: RFC 3629 (STD 63, November 2003), which obsoletes RFC 2279. ISO/IEC 10646 Annex D also describes it.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › UTF-8 definition (RFC 3629 + Unicode FAQ)

units.text: • U+0000 .. U+007F (US-ASCII) map to single bytes 00 .. 7F. A plain ASCII string is valid UTF-8. • US-ASCII byte values do not appear inside a non-ASCII UTF-8 character. Parsers that look for ASCII syntax (slash, space, NUL) do not get false ASCII from later bytes of a multi-byte character. • One to four bytes per character in the U+0000 .. U+10FFFF range. • The first byte of a multi-byte sequence tells the length. • Octet values C0, C1, F5-FF never appear in well-formed UTF-8. • Character boundaries can be found from the byte stream. • overlong encodings are illegal (e.g. C0 80 is not U+0000).
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › UTF-8 definition (RFC 3629 + Unicode FAQ)

units.text: There is only one valid way to encode a given character. Implementations MUST refuse invalid sequences. A naive decoder that accepts overlong forms or surrogate pairs as UTF-8 is a security bug. RFC 3629 records real exploits that used illegal sequences to sneak ../ and NUL past filters.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › UTF-8 definition (RFC 3629 + Unicode FAQ)

units.text: CESU-8 encodes UTF-16 code units instead of code points. It is not valid UTF-8 and is not for the internet.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › UTF-8 definition (RFC 3629 + Unicode FAQ)

units.text: UTF-8 has no endianness. A BOM in UTF-8 is only a signature that the file is UTF-8, not a byte-order switch. The UTF-8 BOM bytes are EF BB BF (Unicode BOM FAQ table). Some protocols (Unix #! scripts, protocols that require a given ASCII start) should not use a UTF-8 BOM.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › UTF-8 definition (RFC 3629 + Unicode FAQ)

units.text: Unicode FAQ : where a BOM is used with UTF-8, it has nothing to do with byte order.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › UTF-8 definition (RFC 3629 + Unicode FAQ)

units.text: encoding form: UTF-32, big-endian
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › BOM table (Unicode FAQ, fetched)

units.text: encoding form: UTF-32, little-endian
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › BOM table (Unicode FAQ, fetched)

units.text: encoding form: UTF-16, big-endian
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › BOM table (Unicode FAQ, fetched)

units.text: encoding form: UTF-16, little-endian
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › BOM table (Unicode FAQ, fetched)

units.text: encoding form: UTF-8
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › BOM table (Unicode FAQ, fetched)

units.text: In the middle of a file, U+FEFF is historically ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE. Unicode prefers U+2060 WORD JOINER for word-joining, so U+FEFF can be a signature without confusion. Fetch the FAQ if a file is full of mystery FEFF.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › BOM table (Unicode FAQ, fetched)

units.text: Tagged UTF-16BE / UTF-16LE / UTF-32BE / UTF-32LE streams must not use a BOM. The tag already named the order.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › BOM table (Unicode FAQ, fetched)

units.topic: character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit
units.text: Four different meters. Mixing them is how software eats a name.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit

units.text: counts: Octets on disk or wire
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit

units.text: counts: 8-bit (UTF-8), 16-bit (UTF-16), or 32-bit (UTF-32) units
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit

units.text: counts: Unicode scalar identity
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit

units.text: counts: What a user thinks of as "a character" (base + combining marks, many emoji sequences)
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit

units.topic: character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit
units.text: A combining sequence (base + acute, a flag emoji of several code points, a Korean syllable as jamo) is one user-perceived character and several code points. Unicode UAX #29 (text segmentation) is the door for grapheme clusters. If you index "the nth character" in a UI, you almost certainly wanted grapheme clusters, not code units.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit

units.topic: character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit
units.text: Do not invent the code points of those sequences here. Fetch.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › character vs grapheme vs byte vs code unit

units.text: Unicode is not a font. Not a language. Not a keyboard. Not a locale. Not a grammar. Not a translation memory.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is not

units.text: Collation (sort order) is language-specific. UTF-8 byte order is not a cultural sort (RFC 3629 says this outright). Fetch the Unicode Collation Algorithm (UTS #10) and CLDR if you must sort names for humans.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is not

units.text: Normalization (NFC, NFD, ...) is UAX #15. Needed when one precomposed accented letter must match a base letter plus combining mark for identity. Fetch it. Do not roll your own.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is not

units.text: Check: encoding named (UTF-8?). Sequence well-formed? comparing bytes, code points, or graphemes? specific U+.... fetched from Unicode, not remembered.
units.section: Digital Text: The Architecture of Unicode and UTF-8 Encodings › what Unicode is not

units.topic: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity
units.text: This chapter is English school grammar for making sentences that do the job. It is not a claim that English is language. It is not a morality. Other languages have other agreements, other tense systems, other places for modifiers. If the text is not English, fetch a grammar of that language.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity

units.topic: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity
units.text: Style-book fights (Oxford comma as a religion, "they" as singular) belong to a named publication style. US literature classrooms often default to MLA; other fields to Chicago. Those manuals are products. This book teaches the clause. For a word's existence and sense, Merriam-Webster. For a character, Unicode.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity

units.text: A clause has a predicate (usually a finite verb) and, in English declaratives, a subject.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › the clause

units.text: • independent clause: can stand as a sentence. • dependent (subordinate) clause: cannot; it hangs on another clause (because ..., who ..., that ...).
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › the clause

units.text: Sentence types by job: declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamative. A period does not make a clause complete. "Running down the road." is a phrase wearing a capital letter.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › the clause

units.text: Simple sentence: one independent clause. compound: coordinated independents. complex: independent + subordinate. Names help you punctuate. They are not a scoring system.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › the clause

units.text: Fragment: a group punctuated as a sentence that is not an independent clause. Illegal in many formal registers. Legal as a rhetorical punch (ch 7). Know which register you are in.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › the clause

units.text: Run-on: two independents jammed without coordination or a fit stop. A comma between independents with no coordinator is a comma splice. Both are clause-boundary failures.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › the clause

units.text: Method : find the finite verbs. Draw the clause boundaries. Then punctuate.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › the clause

units.text: English default declarative order is SVO. That is a default, not a cage: questions invert, relatives front, passives promote objects.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › subject, verb, object, complement

units.text: a singular subject takes a singular verb form where English still marks it (the box is; the boxes are). Traps:
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › subject, verb, object, complement

units.text: • intervening phrases do not change the head: the box of nails is (head = box). • coordination: and usually plural; or agrees with the nearer conjunct in many school rules — fetch the style book if the sentence is on trial. • collective nouns (committee, team) vary by variety (US often singular, some UK usage plural when the members act separately). Name the variety. • there is / there are: the delayed noun is the agreement controller in the school rule: there are three reasons. • none, data, media: usage is shifting; a dictionary + a style book beat a remembered prohibition.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › subject, verb, object, complement

units.text: Case in English is thin: I/me, he/him, who/whom as the surviving school set. After a preposition, object form (between you and me). whom is formal; many registers use who. Do not fake a whom and miss the clause.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › subject, verb, object, complement

units.text: Complement: what completes the verb. be and other linking verbs take a subject complement (she is the chair), not an object. Confusing those two makes bad case and bad passives.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › subject, verb, object, complement

units.text: Tense locates the situation in time (English: past vs non-past as the marked morphological pair). aspect is the internal shape (ongoing, completed, habitual). modality is necessity, possibility, obligation (must, may, should, and periphrasis).
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: typical form: walks; typical job: Habit, general fact, scheduled future, live report
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: typical form: is walking; typical job: Ongoing now, temporary, arranged future
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: typical form: walked; typical job: Completed in a past time
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: typical form: was walking; typical job: Ongoing in the past
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: typical form: has walked; typical job: Past with present relevance
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: typical form: had walked; typical job: Earlier than another past
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: typical form: will walk; typical job: Future as prediction or intention (not a morphological tense)
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: Do not use past perfect just because the event is "very past." use it when one past is before another past the reader must keep.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: Sequence of tenses in reported speech is a register habit, not physics.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: Passive (was written) promotes the patient, demotes or drops the agent. It is a tool. It is not inherently cowardly. It is cowardly when it hides an agent the reader is owed.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.text: Subjunctive remnants: if I were, that she see. Rare. Do not spray them.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › tense, aspect, modality

units.topic: modifiers — put them where they belong
units.text: A modifier should sit next to what it modifies. English is unforgiving here because it has little case.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › modifiers — put them where they belong

units.topic: modifiers — put them where they belong
units.text: Misplaced modifier: I wrote about the dog in my pyjamas — who is wearing the pyjamas? move the phrase.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › modifiers — put them where they belong

units.topic: modifiers — put them where they belong
units.text: Dangling modifier: an introductory phrase whose implied subject is not the grammatical subject. Walking down the street, the building exploded. the building was not walking. Fix the subject or rewrite.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › modifiers — put them where they belong

units.text: only attaches to the next eligible unit. I only tested three cases vs I tested only three cases. Put only against the thing you mean to limit.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › modifiers — put them where they belong

units.text: usually no commas; that or which in US school fights; many UK styles allow which without commas for restrictive. Fetch the style book; do not invent a universal.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › modifiers — put them where they belong

units.text: commas; which (or who). The commas are meaning.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › modifiers — put them where they belong

units.topic: modifiers — put them where they belong
units.text: Participial phrases after a noun attach to that noun. the man eating a sandwich vs the man, eating a sandwich, ... — punctuation changes the job.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › modifiers — put them where they belong

units.topic: modifiers — put them where they belong
units.text: Stacking adjectives: English has a preferred order (opinion, size, age, color, origin, material, purpose as a school mnemonic). Native speakers hear a violation. If a string of adjectives creaks, reorder or split.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › modifiers — put them where they belong

units.text: Parallelism: coordinated pieces should share a shape. to err is human; to forgive, divine works because both sides are infinitival. she likes hiking, to swim, and bikes does not.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › parallelism, reference, and noise

units.text: Pronoun reference: a pronoun needs an unambiguous antecedent. they as a singular generic is ordinary English; make the antecedent clear anyway. this at the start of a sentence with no noun is a fog machine — this claim, this result.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › parallelism, reference, and noise

units.text: Agreement in number with everyone, each: school formal English treats them as singular (everyone has his or her / everyone has their — pick a style and hold it).
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › parallelism, reference, and noise

units.text: Double negative as agreement vs as logic: in many English varieties I don't know nothing is negative concord (still one negation). In standard written English it is read as a logic error or a dialect feature you did not mean to signal. Know the register.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › parallelism, reference, and noise

units.text: Check: finite verb found. Clause boundary drawn. Agreement with the head. Modifier touching its noun. only next to the limited thing. Pronoun has one antecedent.
units.section: Applied Grammar for Authors: Clauses, Voice, and Syntactic Clarity › parallelism, reference, and noise

units.topic: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style
units.text: Rhetoric is the craft of moving an audience. The literature pack owns the long form (../literature/ ch 11). This pack owns the linguistic overlap: a sentence is already a speech act (ch 2.6).
units.section: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style

units.topic: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style
units.text: Aristotle's school triad: ethos (why this speaker may be believed), pathos (what feeling is stirred), logos (what follows). Fetch the Rhetoric on Perseus if you will quote it. The canons (invention, arrangement, style, memory, delivery) are a later Roman school list.
units.section: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style

units.topic: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style
units.text: Register is the first rhetorical choice a linguist can name: who is to be moved, on what occasion (kairos). A clause that is grammatical and still wrong for the occasion is a pragmatic miss, not a syntax miss.
units.section: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style

units.topic: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style
units.text: • anaphora: repeat at the left edge. • parallelism: ch 6.5 as rhetoric, not only as correctness. • antithesis: two clauses set against each other. • rhetorical question: an interrogative doing an assertion. • passive and nominalization: hide or highlight agents.
units.section: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style

units.topic: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style
units.text: Literature pack : tropes [metaphor, irony] and close reading. This chapter: do not call a grammatical failure a style. fix the clause, then decide whether the fragment is a punch.
units.section: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style

units.topic: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style
units.text: Check: who is to be moved. By which means. On which occasion. The literature pack if the object is a novel or a speech as art.
units.section: Rhetorical Structures: Persuasion, Coherence, and Style

units.topic: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words
units.text: Lexicography is how dictionaries are made: evidence of use, then a definition. etymology is the history of a form. They are different jobs.
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words

units.text: • write the form you actually have (spelling, capitalization, morphology). A declined or inflected form may need the citation form (went → go). • open a dictionary that names its evidence. for contemporary US English, Merriam-Webster is the public door this pack names. Historical sense, first dates, and finer splits often need a historical dictionary (OED is a product; fetch if you have it).
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words › method (lookup)

units.text: Bilingual jobs need a bilingual dictionary plus a monolingual in the source language. • read the whole entry: part of speech, numbered senses, examples, usage labels (dated, slang, technical, offensive). • pick the sense that fits this sentence. do not paste sense 1 into a sentence that wanted sense 4. • If two reputable dictionaries disagree, say so. Do not average them.
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words › method (lookup)

units.text: Collocation: words that habitually sit together (make a decision, strong tea). A synonym that breaks the collocation is not a synonym in use.
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words › method (lookup)

units.text: Corpus check: if the job is "do people say this," a dictionary example is a start; a corpus (or honest search in a named collection) is better. Do not take a comment-section majority as a corpus.
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words › method (lookup)

units.text: Folk etymology is a story that sounds like history: history from his story; avocado from a tale you just coined; nice "originally" meaning a moral you need for a sermon.
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words › what not to do (folk etymology)

units.text: • An etymology without a cited dictionary or historical grammar is a guess. • cognates are related by descent, not by meaning today. Resemblance across languages is not a shared soul. Fetch the dictionary; do not preach from a rhyme. • false friends are lookalikes across languages with different meanings. They are a translation hazard (ch 9). • acronym lore (posh as a steamship ticket, and cousins) is almost always false. If an acronym origin is real, a dictionary will say so. • oldest meaning owns us is a fallacy. Etymology does not police today's sense. Fetch the usage note, then decide for this register. History is not a warrant.
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words › what not to do (folk etymology)

units.text: Morphological transparency (un-happy) is not etymology. It is living structure (ch 2.3). A word can be morphologically opaque and still current (cranberry).
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words › what not to do (folk etymology)

units.text: Check: dictionary named, sense numbered, etymology only if the dictionary or a historical grammar funded it. Empty hit → state unverified. Never invent a root.
units.section: Lexicography and Etymology: The Biography of Words › what not to do (folk etymology)

units.topic: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss
units.text: Translation maps meaning and job from a source language into a target language. It is not a column of dictionary equivalents.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss

units.text: • sense inventories differ. a source word with four senses is not four copies of one target word. • grammar differs. a language that marks evidentiality, honorifics, or dual number forces the translator to add or drop distinctions English does not mark. • collocation and idiom are not compositional (ch 2.5). kick the bucket word-swapped is a kick and a bucket. • register and speech act (ch 2.6, ch 7). A polite formula swapped literally becomes rude or comic. • names and culture. a food, a legal office, a kinship term may have no one-word target. gloss, loan, or explain — pick on purpose.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss › why word-swap fails

units.text: Calque (loan translation) copies structure. Sometimes it works (loanword itself is a calque of German Lehnwort). Sometimes it produces English nobody asked for.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss › why word-swap fails

units.text: False friends: see ch 8. A shared Latin ancestor is not a shared sense.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss › why word-swap fails

units.text: • read the source as a text (genre, speaker, clause, implicature). Literature pack if it is art. • name the job in the target (legal force, joke, warning, lyric). • translate clauses, not words. Keep argument structure unless the target grammar requires a rebuild. • then choose words that carry the sense and the register. • If a wording is load-bearing (a statute, a poem, a UI string, a religious text), fetch the source and say what you cannot carry.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss › method

units.text: Machine translation is a draft. It word-swaps at industrial scale, with fluent cover. check every proper name, negation, number, and scope. A missing not is a different speech act.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss › method

units.text: Localization is translation plus locale: date formats, decimal marks, honorifics, legal copy, layout (W3C i18n). Encoding is UTF-8 (ch 5). Language tags are BCP 47 (ch 12). None of those is the translation itself.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss › method

units.text: Back-translation is a check, not a proof. If the back-translation is identical, you may have written English wearing a costume.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss › method

units.text: Check: source language named. Target register named. What could not be carried is stated. No invented proverb.
units.section: The Theory of Translation: Equivalence, Fidelity, and Pragmatic Loss › method

units.text: Everybody speaks a variety. standard is a variety with institutions (schools, offices, publishers). It is not the language's essence.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › variation

units.text: Accent is pronunciation. dialect includes grammar and lexicon. code-switching is moving between systems on purpose. None of these is "broken."
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › variation

units.text: Prestige and stigma are social facts. They are not phonology.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › variation

units.text: When a writer's job is standard written English, say so and use ch 6. When the job is to describe a variety, describe it. Do not "correct" a transcript of speech into a textbook and call it the data.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › variation

units.text: Languages change. sound change, analogy, borrowing, grammaticalization (content word to grammatical piece) are school names. diachrony (ch 3) is this cut.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › change

units.text: Relatedness is family descent (Romance, Germanic, Bantu as names of families), not "they look similar." regular sound correspondence is the method. Resemblance without correspondence is a guess. Do not invent a proto-form.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › change

units.text: Contact: pidgins, creoles, mixed varieties, areal features. A creole is a language. It is not a failed standard.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › change

units.text: Fetch a historical grammar for a reconstruction. This book will not reconstruct Proto-Indo-European on a dare.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › change

units.text: Children build a grammar from the language around them, without being taught the six cuts. critical period talk is a research program — fetch a survey, do not cite a remembered age as law.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › acquisition

units.text: Second-language learning is not first-language acquisition with worse luck. It has transfer, instruction, and adult attention.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › acquisition

units.text: MIT OCW 24.900 Introduction to Linguistics is the undergrad door this pack names for acquisition, historical change, and signed languages as course objects.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › acquisition

units.text: Check: variety named. Change claimed only with a source. Acquisition claims fetched, not remembered from a magazine.
units.section: Sociolinguistics, Dialectology, and First Language Acquisition › acquisition

units.topic: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles
units.text: Noam Chomsky's program (from the 1950s onward) is a theory of what a grammar is, not a writing handbook and not an official web standard. There is no Chomsky URL in this pack's index. If you need a page, fetch a paper or a textbook citation. Do not invent a homepage and call it primary authority.
units.section: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles

units.topic: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles
units.text: • A grammar is a finite system that generates unbounded expressions (the "infinite use of finite means" slogan is older; the generative cut is explicit mechanism). • I-language: the internal state of a speaker. E-language: external corpora, social objects. The theory's object is I-language.
units.section: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles

units.text: the theory is about competence. Slips, memory limits, and corpus frequencies are performance unless you have a theory that joins them.
units.section: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles

units.topic: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles
units.text: • universal grammar (UG): the hypothesis that humans come with a specifically linguistic initial state. This is a research program, not a list of universals you can paste. poverty of the stimulus is the named argument that the data underdetermine the grammar the child reaches. Philosophers and psychologists fight this (SEP: philosophy of linguistics, language and innateness).
units.section: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles

units.topic: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles
units.text: Do not pretend the fight is over. • syntactic structure is real: constituency, movement, hierarchical embedding — trees, not only word chains. colorless green ideas sleep furiously is the school sentence for "grammatical but semantically odd." • Later names (Government and Binding, Minimalist Program, merge) are stages of the same family. You do not need them to write English. You need them to read a syntax paper.
units.section: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles

units.topic: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles
units.text: • Not "Chomsky said never use the passive." • Not a spellchecker. • Not a claim that all languages have English parts of speech under English names. • Not a URL.
units.section: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles

units.topic: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles
units.text: Descriptive vs prescriptive: generative grammar is descriptive of I-language. Ch 6 is prescriptive for a written register on purpose. Keep the hats off each other's heads.
units.section: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles

units.topic: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles
units.text: Check: are you describing a speaker's system, or editing a page? if editing, ch 6. If theorizing, name the claim so it can be wrong.
units.section: Generative Grammar and Universal Linguistic Principles

units.topic: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags
units.text: Computers and catalogs need tags. Humans need names. They are not the same.
units.section: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags

units.topic: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags
units.text: BCP 47 (IETF Best Current Practice 47) is how the internet tags languages. It currently includes RFC 5646 (tags) and RFC 4647 (matching). W3C tells authors to choose a language tag and put it on HTML (lang). Fetch W3C "Choosing a Language Tag" and the IANA Language Subtag Registry. Do not invent a subtag.
units.section: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags

units.topic: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags
units.text: School shape of a tag (read the RFC for the grammar): a primary language subtag, then optional script, region, variant subtags, hyphen-separated. Examples belong on the IANA registry and W3C's article — fetch them for the language you have. A two-letter code you remember from high school may be ISO 639-1 and still be the wrong tag for the variety on the page.
units.section: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags

units.topic: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags
units.text: ISO 639 language codes: the Library of Congress is the coding agency for ISO 639-2 (Set 2). That LoC page is the authorized list for those three-letter codes. ISO 639-3 aims at comprehensive coverage of individual languages; it is a different set with a different agency. do not treat Ethnologue's product pages as the free public primary authority for a code. If you need a catalog of languoids and references, Glottolog is a research catalog (Max Planck). Speaker counts rot; fetch and date them.
units.section: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags

units.topic: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags
units.text: Macro-languages and language vs dialect (ch 1) reappear here as tag fights. A tag is an identifier for an information object. It is not a political recognition of a people. Still: tagging a person with the wrong language is a practical harm. Pick the tag that matches the text.
units.section: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags

units.topic: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags
units.text: Check: tag fetched from IANA / W3C / LoC. Script subtag only if the script is not the default. No homemade codes.
units.section: Standardization and Identification: BCP 47 and ISO 639 Language Tags
