units.topic: Software Engineering & Architecture — System Specification, Invariant Design, Distributed Versioning & Resilient Delivery
units.text: A comprehensive undergraduate textbook exploring the principles and practices of modern software engineering : formal specifications, invariant-driven design, cryptographic version control via Merkle DAGs, automated test harnesses, network protocols [HTTP/1.1–HTTP/3], data serialization standards, relational persistence, failure domains, and zero-defect deployment pipelines.

units.topic: The First Principles of Software Engineering
units.text: Consider an ordinary elevator in an office building. When you press the button for the fourth floor, the light turns on. The motor activates, the elevator car rises smoothly to the fourth floor, the doors slide open, and the button light turns off.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering

units.topic: The First Principles of Software Engineering
units.text: Now imagine if the elevator occasionally took you to the basement when you pressed the roof, or forgot your button press unless you tapped it three times, or opened its doors between floors while moving. In physical machines, we would call that a mechanical failure. But in software, we call such things "bugs"—even though software has no gears that wear down, no bearings that seize, and no belts that snap.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering

units.topic: The First Principles of Software Engineering
units.text: Because software is not a physical contraption; it is a formal specification of logic and state. When a program misbehaves, it is almost never because the computer got tired or the electricity was dirty. It fails because the instructions written by humans were contradictory, incomplete, or made fragile assumptions about the world that crumbled when reality intervened.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering

units.topic: The First Principles of Software Engineering
units.text: Software engineering is the disciplined craft of designing digital machines that do exactly what the package says, remain maintainable over years of change, and fail safely when the unexpected occurs. It is not "typing until it compiles," and it is not about chasing trendy frameworks. It is an unbroken chain: intent → specification → implementation → automated proof → delivery → observation.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering

units.text: • State and Transitions (The Scoreboard): Think of a basketball arena scoreboard. At any given moment, the scoreboard displays a snapshot of the game: Home: 42, Away: 39, Period: 3, Clock: 4:15. That snapshot is called state. When a player sinks a free throw, a single number increments to 43. That controlled update is a state transition. If a player scores and the clock unexpectedly resets to 12:00 while the Away score vanishes, the scoreboard's state transitions are corrupt. A software engineer's first duty is to precisely define valid states and ensure only legitimate events can trigger transitions between them.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: • The Invariant (The Sacred Rule): An invariant is a physical or logical condition that must remain true through every single operation. In a bank account system, the invariant is absolute: after a money transfer, the sender's account must decrease by the exact sum the recipient's account increases. Even if the network drops mid-transaction, power blinks, or two users click transfer at the same millisecond, money cannot magically evaporate or duplicate. Engineers design invariants first, and construct code to protect them.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: • Failing Closed (The Emergency Brake): On a railway train, the air brake system is pressurized. If a pipe tears or pressure drops, heavy mechanical springs automatically force the brake shoes against the wheels, bringing the train to a halt. The system fails closed (or fail-safe). In software, when an error occurs—an unparseable data packet, an unknown user ID, an unreachable database—the system must never guess, fabricate dummy data, or pretend success. It must fail closed: halt the risky operation, roll back changes, preserve data integrity, and surface an unambiguous error.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: • Verifiable Proof (Engineering vs. a Demo): A demo is something that worked once on the developer's personal laptop under ideal conditions. Engineering leaves a reproducible trail of evidence: written specifications, automated test suites that run in fresh environments, structured logs, and cryptographic version control. If a stranger on the other side of the world cannot clone your repository, run the verification harness, and observe identical behavior, you have a demo, not an engineering artifact.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: everyday reality: The promise; what it proves: A checkable claim about what the software does for the user
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: everyday reality: The mechanism; what it proves: The code, configuration, and data structures built to fulfill the promise
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: everyday reality: The receipt; what it proves: Automated test runs, reproducible traces, and diffs proving the claim is met
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: The Law of Done: Software that cannot be independently checked is not finished. A comment saying "this should work" is a hope, not a proof. A green status badge whose test command was commented out is a stub claiming completion.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: The First Practice: Take any feature or script you wrote recently. Formulate a single falsifiable statement: "This system is correct if and only if ______." If you cannot complete that sentence without vague hand-waving, your specification does not exist yet. Chapter 2 shows how to write one.
units.section: The First Principles of Software Engineering › The Four Core Intuitions

units.text: Definition. a spec is a checkable claim about behaviour. It names inputs, outputs, errors, and what stays unchanged. It is short. It is not a novel. It is not the code.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: question: Who calls this? human, another service, a cron
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: question: What is true before
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: question: The action (HTTP method + path, button, CLI verb)
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: question: Observable result (status, body, file, UI)
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: question: How it fails closed (4xx/5xx, thrown error, rollback)
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: question: What must not move (other rows, other users’ data)
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Why before how. if you start at how, you will invent a stack and then hunt for a problem that fits it. Name the job in the user’s words. Then pick the smallest mechanism.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Acceptance is a test, not a vibe. “feels fast” is not acceptance. “p95 under 200 ms on this fixture” is, and then you measure. Numbers you did not measure → state unverified / fetch / calc.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Invariants. an invariant is a sentence that stays true across calls. Examples: “every order has exactly one owner”; “GET does not create a row”; “retrying a paid invoice does not charge twice.” write invariants in the spec. Tests encode them. Logs prove you looked.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Interface first. the public surface (function signature, HTTP resource, CLI) is the contract. Internals may change. If two hosts (desktop, browser, phone) claim the same job, they use the same names for the same operations. Renaming per platform is a second product.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Scope cut. a spec that lists twelve features is a wishlist. Cut to the one path that teaches the system. Ship that. Then the next. Unfinished code that claims done is a stub: finish it or mark it blocked. Do not sign off an outline as a program.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Fail closed on the unknown. unknown unit, unknown origin, unknown tool name → error. Inventing a 1:1 conversion or a 200 OK for a bad request is a lie with a green status.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Job : “user can add a unit conversion to a note.”
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Bad spec : “build a conversion feature with a nice UI.”
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: • Given a note open and a number selected • When the user asks to convert 5 km to miles • Then the note shows the converted value from the units hand, not from the model’s memory • Fail: unknown unit → error string, note unchanged • Unchanged: other notes, any secret store
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: EasyLM’s calc and units hands are this pattern: arithmetic is a tool with a spec, not a fluent guess. The Stacks returns a chapter. The model does not invent the constant.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.text: Check. if a teammate can implement the spec without asking what “success” looks like, the spec is ready. If they have to guess the status code, it is not. Write the failing test or the refused case before the happy path.
units.section: Specification Before Implementation & Invariant Design

units.topic: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood
units.text: Facts in this chapter come from the Git book at git-scm, not from folklore. Door: https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood

units.text: Definition. Git is a content-addressable filesystem with a version-control user interface on top. At the core it is a key-value store: you insert content, Git hands back a key (a hash of a typed header plus the content), and you retrieve by that key.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: Git stores snapshots, not a list of diffs as the primary object. A commit points at a tree (the project snapshot). The next commit points at the previous commit (its parent) and at a new tree.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: is: The contents of a file. No filename inside the blob
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: is: A directory listing: mode, type, hash, filename; each entry a blob or another tree
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: is: Pointer to a tree, zero or more parent commits, author, committer, message
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: is: A named pointer, often annotated, to a commit
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: Git writes each object as a header (blob <size>\0 or tree … or commit …) plus content, then hashes that, historically with SHA-1 (40 hex characters). The object file lives under .git/objects/ab/… where ab is the first two hex digits. Git may later pack objects; the logical model does not change. SHA-256 repositories exist as a format; if you need which hash a given repo uses, inspect that repo, do not guess.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: The Git book’s own example: echo 'test content' | git hash-object -w --stdin stores a blob and prints d670460b4b4aece5915caf5c68d12f560a9fe3e4. git cat-file -p of that hash prints test content. git cat-file -t prints blob. If you need a hash for your file, compute it with Git on this box; do not reuse the book’s hash as if it were yours.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: Zero parents on the first commit. One parent on a normal commit. Two parents on a merge commit.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: Law. the hash is of the object bytes, not of the filename. Rename a file: new tree, same blob if contents did not change. Change one byte: new blob, new hash.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: Check. git cat-file -t HEAD and git cat-file -p HEAD. You should see a commit that names a tree. Then git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree} (quoting as your shell requires) lists names. If you cannot find a blob for a file you committed, you are looking at the working tree, not the object database.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › what git is

units.text: Definition. a branch in Git is a lightweight movable pointer to a commit (Git book: Branches in a Nutshell). It is a file under .git/refs/heads/ whose content is a commit hash (or a packed-ref). It is not a copy of the project.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › branch

units.text: HEAD is a pointer to the current branch (or, in detached HEAD, to a commit). git branch testing creates a new pointer at the current commit. It does not switch. git switch testing or git checkout testing moves HEAD to that branch.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › branch

units.text: The default name created by git init has historically been master. Git itself does not treat that name as magic; it is a branch like any other. Many hosts now default to main. The fact is the pointer, not the label.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › branch

units.text: Law. creating a branch is cheap because it writes a hash. It does not copy trees. Two branch names on the same commit are two pointers, not two copies.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › branch

units.text: Check. git log --oneline --decorate. You should see HEAD -> on the branch you have checked out, and other names sitting on commits.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › branch

units.text: Definition. a merge joins two lines of history. Git finds a common ancestor, diffs each side against it, and applies both sets of changes. If the result is clean, Git can make a merge commit: a commit with two parents. If both sides changed the same region, Git stops and asks you to resolve.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › merge

units.text: A fast-forward is the special case where one side has no unique commits : Git just slides the branch pointer forward. No merge commit is required.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › merge

units.text: Law. merge preserves the commits that existed on both sides. It adds a node that points at both tips. It does not rewrite those commits.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › merge

units.text: Check. after git merge other, git cat-file -p HEAD should show two parent lines if it was a true merge. git log --graph --oneline should show the join. If you see one parent, it was a fast-forward (or you merged nothing).
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › merge

units.text: Definition. rebase takes the patch of each commit on your branch that is not on the new base, and replays those patches on top of the new base. The result is new commit objects (new hashes, new parents). The old commits remain in the object database until garbage-collected; the branch pointer moves to the replayed tip.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › rebase

units.text: From the Git book (Branching — Rebasing): rebase is a way to make a linear story. It is also a way to rewrite history that other people may have built on.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › rebase

units.text: Law. do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that others may have based work on. Rewriting a published tip forces everyone else to recover. Merge is the cooperative default on a shared branch. Rebase is for local cleanup before you share, or for a workflow the whole team has agreed.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › rebase

units.text: Check. after a rebase onto main, git log main..HEAD should show your commits with new hashes sitting on the current main. git merge-base HEAD main should be the tip of main if the rebase was complete. If a colleague still has the old hashes, you rewrote published history — stop and recover, do not force-push as a reflex.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › rebase

units.text: is: Files on disk you edit
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › working tree, index, HEAD

units.text: is: What the next commit will contain
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › working tree, index, HEAD

units.text: is: The last commit on the current branch
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › working tree, index, HEAD

units.text: git add copies working-tree bytes into a blob and records the name in the index. git commit writes a tree from the index and a commit pointing at it. git restore / git reset move content between these three; they are not synonyms. Fetch the Git book “Reset Demystified” if you are about to run reset --hard on uncommitted work.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › working tree, index, HEAD

units.text: Check. git status names the three areas in English. If status is dirty and you cannot say whether the bytes live in the index or only on disk, do not commit yet.
units.section: The Merkle DAG: How Git Actually Works Under the Hood › working tree, index, HEAD

units.text: Definition. a remote is a named URL of another repository. origin is only a convention. git fetch copies objects and updates remote-tracking refs (origin/main). git pull is fetch plus a merge or rebase. git push updates a branch on the remote to point at a commit you have, sending missing objects.
units.section: Distributed Collaboration: Remotes, Branches & Evidence

units.text: Law. the remote does not magically contain your working tree. Uncommitted bytes are not backed up by push. A green “synced” icon on a dirty tree is a lie. git status clean on the branch you meant to ship is the evidence.
units.section: Distributed Collaboration: Remotes, Branches & Evidence

units.text: Force-push. git push --force (and --force-with-lease) moves a remote branch pointer to a commit that may not be a descendant of what was there. On a shared main, that is how you lose the evidence other people pulled. --force-with-lease still rewrites; it only refuses if the remote moved since you last fetched. It is not a licence to rewrite public history.
units.section: Distributed Collaboration: Remotes, Branches & Evidence

units.text: Messages. a commit message says why. The diff says what. “fix” and “wip” are not why.
units.section: Distributed Collaboration: Remotes, Branches & Evidence

units.text: Check. after push, clone into a fresh directory and run the test command from the README. If that clone cannot run, you did not ship a repository; you shipped a laptop state.
units.section: Distributed Collaboration: Remotes, Branches & Evidence

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Definition. a test is a machine-runnable claim about a spec. Fail closed means: if the claim is false, or the test cannot run, the change does not ship. Fail open means: a skip, a swallowed exception, a missing file, or a flaky retry that eventually greens, and the change ships anyway.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Law. the default is fail closed. An empty test suite that “passes” is fail open. A test that mocks the entire system and asserts true is fail open. A CI job that is allowed to fail is fail open for that job.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: inc(3) is 4, so the assertion fails and pytest exits non-zero. That is the point. The test is not decoration; it is the gate.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.text: job: One function, in-process; typical fail: Wrong return, thrown type
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.text: job: HTTP/JSON/SQL shape; typical fail: 500, malformed body, missing column
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.text: job: Two real pieces; typical fail: Timeout, schema drift
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.text: job: A user path; typical fail: UI missing, auth broken
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Do not start at end-to-end. An e2e suite that cannot name the unit that broke is a fog machine.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Write the failing test first when the spec is new. See red. Then write the minimum code that turns it green. Then see red again if you break it. A test written after the code that only repeats the implementation is a snapshot, not a spec.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Determinism. a test that depends on clock, network, or unordered maps without a seed will flake. Freeze time, fake the network at a seam, sort when order is not the spec. Flaky tests train humans to ignore red — that is fail open.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Coverage is not the goal. a 100% line-covered function can still be wrong if no assertion names the invariant. Prefer one sharp assertion per claim over a carpet of existence checks. Coverage percent is not a spec. A fully covered wrong conversion is still wrong.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Names. refuses_unknown_unit_pairs is a claim. test1 is not.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Worked check. spec: parse_int("12") returns integer 12; parse_int("x") fails closed (error, no silent 0).
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: If parse_int returns 0 on junk, the second test is the one that catches it. The first test alone is fail open on the error path.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: EasyLM’s own bar, as a worked product example: unknown units error; they do not invent 1:1. The Stacks miss says miss. Those are tests you can write without a browser. Calc does arithmetic; the model does not.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed
units.text: Check. delete the implementation; the test must go red. If it stays green, it was not testing the thing. Run the suite until it fails on purpose (break the code). If nothing goes red, you do not have a test. You have a script that prints ok.
units.section: Automated Verification: Tests That Fail Closed

units.topic: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP
units.text: Door : https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110 — HTTP Semantics, June 2022, STD 97, Fielding, Nottingham, Reschke. This RFC is the semantics shared by HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3. Wire syntax lives in other RFCs [9112, 9113, 9114]. If a blog and this RFC disagree, the RFC wins.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP

units.topic: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP
units.text: Definition. HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol. A client sends a request with a method and a target resource. A server returns a status code and, often, a representation (bytes plus metadata). The protocol does not define your database. It defines the uniform interface.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP

units.text: is: The target of a request, identified by a URI
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP

units.text: is: Bytes + metadata that stand for a state of the resource
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP

units.text: is: The program that can answer authoritatively for that URI
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP

units.text: is: Essentially read-only; no obligation to change state (§9.2.1)
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP

units.text: is: N identical requests have the same effect as one (§9.2.2)
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP

units.topic: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP
units.text: URI schemes : http default TCP port 80; https default TCP port 443, with TLS. An origin is scheme + host + port after normalisation [RFC 9110 §4.3.1]. https://Example.Com/happy.js has origin { "https", "example.com", "443" }. Two origins that differ in scheme, host, or port are distinct.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP

units.text: intent: Transfer a current representation of the target resource; safe: Yes; idempotent: Yes
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: intent: Like GET, but the server does not send content; safe: Yes; idempotent: Yes
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: intent: Process the request content according to the resource’s own semantics (often create or append); safe: No; idempotent: No
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: intent: Replace the target resource with the enclosed representation; safe: No; idempotent: Yes
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: intent: Remove the association between the target resource and its current functionality; safe: No; idempotent: Yes
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: intent: Establish a tunnel to the origin; safe: No; idempotent: No
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: intent: Request communication options for the target; safe: Yes; idempotent: Yes
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: intent: Message loop-back for diagnostics; safe: Yes; idempotent: Yes
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: PATCH (partial update) is defined in RFC 5789, not as a core method of RFC 9110. If you implement PATCH, fetch RFC 5789. Do not invent “PATCH is like PUT.” PATCH is not required to be idempotent.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: • GET and HEAD must not be used to change server state as part of their contract. A GET that deletes a row is a bug, even if your framework makes it easy. • PUT of the same body twice leaves the resource in the same state (idempotent). POST twice may create two rows. • The method is the verb. The URI is the noun. Do not bury the verb in /api/doCreateUser and then POST to it as theatre. POST /users or PUT /users/{id} is the uniform interface.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: Wrong : GET /invoices/9/pay — GET is safe; paying is not.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: Right : POST /invoices/9/payments with a client-generated idempotency key [chapter 10], so a retry does not pay twice. PUT of a payment resource at a client-chosen URI [PUT /invoices/9/payments/{key}] is also idempotent by construction.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › methods (RFC 9110 §9)

units.text: meaning: Informational; client should: Wait; not the final answer
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: meaning: Success; client should: The request was understood and accepted
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: meaning: Redirection; client should: Look at Location / cache rules
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: meaning: Client error; client should: Fix the request; do not blindly retry as-is
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: meaning: Server error; client should: The server failed; retry only if the method is idempotent and the failure is transient
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: OK; use: GET succeeded; body is the representation
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Created; use: A new resource exists; Location often set
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: No Content; use: Success, empty body (common after DELETE or an empty PUT)
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Not Modified; use: Conditional GET; cache is still good
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Bad Request; use: The request is malformed
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Unauthorized; use: Missing or bad credentials (despite the name: unauthenticated)
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Forbidden; use: Credentials understood, access refused
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Not Found; use: No current representation, or you will not admit it
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Conflict; use: Current state does not allow the method
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Too Many Requests; use: Rate limit
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Internal Server Error; use: The server hit a bug; log it
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Bad Gateway; use: This server, as gateway, got a bad answer upstream
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: name: Service Unavailable; use: Overloaded or down; Retry-After if you know
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: Law. do not return 200 with {"error": ...} as your only signal. Clients, caches, and monitors read the status. A JSON error field is extra; the status is the contract. Do not return 500 for a missing id — that is 404 or 400. Do not return 401 when the user is known and not allowed — that is 403.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.text: Check. for each endpoint, write the method, the success status, and one 4xx. If two endpoints share a method+path and mean different things, the spec is colliding. Fetch RFC 9110 §9 and §15 when you are about to invent a new verb or a new meaning for 200.
units.section: Network Protocols: The Formal Semantics of HTTP › status codes (RFC 9110 §15)

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: Door : https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259 — The JavaScript Object Notation [JSON] Data Interchange Format, December 2017, Bray ed. Obsoletes RFC 7159.
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: Definition. JSON is a text format for structured data. It can represent four primitive types (string, number, boolean, null) and two structured types (object, array). It is language-independent. It is not JavaScript. It is not YAML. It is not “whatever print emitted.”
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: • A JSON text is ws value ws — a single value, optionally padded with insignificant whitespace (space, tab, LF, CR). Older lore that “JSON must be an object or array” is from earlier specs; RFC 8259 allows any value. Generators that only emit object or array stay maximally interoperable. • object: { string : value (, string : value) }. Names SHOULD be unique. Duplicate names make receiver behaviour unpredictable. • array: [ value (, value) ]. Order matters. Types may mix. • number: base-10, optional minus, no leading zeros, optional fraction and exponent.
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: Infinity and NaN are not permitted. • string: Unicode text in double quotes, with the usual escapes. • Literals: true false null — lowercase only.
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: Encoding (RFC 8259 §8.1). JSON text SHALL be encoded in UTF-8. It SHALL NOT begin with a byte order mark.
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: • No comments. No trailing commas. No single quotes. Those are JavaScript / JSONC / JSON5, not JSON. • Object member order is not significant for meaning. If you need order, use an array. • Numbers are decimal text, not IEEE floats, at the JSON layer. Your language will parse them into floats or decimals. Large integers (2^53 and above in IEEE binary64) will silently round in many runtimes. If the id must round-trip, use a string. Money: integers of cents, or a decimal type, not 0.1 + 0.2 in IEEE. calc does the arithmetic. • null is a value. Omitting a key is a different fact. Pick one and document it. • Never build JSON by concatenating user strings. Parse, then pick fields.
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: Schema. if two processes exchange JSON, name the keys and types. Reject extras or missing required keys on the boundary that faces the world.
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: Parse with a real parser (json.loads in Python, JSON.parse in JS). Do not split on commas. Do not eval.
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.topic: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON
units.text: Check. round-trip: parse, serialise, parse again. If a float changes, you have a number-precision problem — switch that field to string or to an integer you can represent, or use calc on the exact decimal. If two official parsers disagree on a document, the document is not interoperable; fix the document.
units.section: Data Serialization: Strict Parsing of RFC 8259 JSON

units.text: Doors : https://www.sqlite.org/docs.html · https://www.sqlite.org/about.html · https://www.sqlite.org/lang.html · https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals

units.text: Definition. SQL is a language for defining and querying relations (tables of rows with named columns). A query names what you want; the engine picks how (mostly). SQLite is an in-process, serverless, zero-configuration, transactional SQL engine that reads and writes a single ordinary file. Public-domain source. Sqlite.org says: think of it as a replacement for fopen(), not as a replacement for a networked cluster database.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals

units.text: From sqlite.org/about (fetched for this book): ACID transactions even after power loss; stable file format; max database size 281 terabytes (2^48 bytes); max row size 1 gigabyte. If a limit is load-bearing for your app, fetch https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html again; do not rely on this paragraph if the live page moved.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals

units.text: A table is a set of rows. A primary key uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key says a value must exist in another table (if you turn enforcement on). A NULL is “unknown / missing,” not the string "null" and not 0 and not ''.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › relational core

units.text: job: Read rows; does not change the database
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › relational core

units.text: job: Add rows
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › relational core

units.text: job: Change columns in existing rows
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › relational core

units.text: job: Remove rows
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › relational core

units.text: Law. write the WHERE before you run UPDATE or DELETE. DELETE FROM t with no WHERE deletes every row. That is not a trick; it is the language. Wrap multi-statement changes in a transaction (BEGIN … COMMIT). If you error, ROLLBACK. SQLite’s ACID claim is about transactions, not about a sequence of autocommit statements you hoped were atomic.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › relational core

units.text: Parameterise. never build SQL by concatenating user strings. Use placeholders (? in SQLite). Concatenation is how injection happens. This is not optional.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › relational core

units.text: If SELECT returns no row, the id does not exist. Do not invent a row in the application to look helpful.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › relational core

units.text: A join combines rows from two tables on a condition, usually a key.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › joins and indexes

units.text: Inner join : only rows that match. If you meant “notes even without tags,” that is a different join [LEFT]. Pick it in the spec, not after the empty result surprises you.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › joins and indexes

units.text: An index is extra structure so a lookup does not scan the whole table. SQLite will use an index when it helps; EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN is how you see. An index is not free: writes maintain it. Index the columns you filter and join on, not every column “just in case.”
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › joins and indexes

units.text: Check. a constraint that can fire. A test that inserts a duplicate primary key and expects failure. A test that EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the hot SELECT does not say “SCAN” of a table you believed was keyed — or you accept the scan in writing.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › joins and indexes

units.text: • One writer at a time on a database file (WAL mode allows concurrent readers). If you need many writers across machines, you need a different engine. Say so; do not pretend. • Types are dynamic with declared type affinity. An INTEGER column can still store text if you bind text. If you need strictness, fetch the current STRICT table docs on sqlite.org; do not guess the version that added them. • INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is an alias for the rowid. That is a SQLite fact; other engines differ. • Backup is “copy the file” only if no writer is in the middle; use the backup API or VACUUM INTO for a consistent snapshot.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › SQLite specifics

units.text: Check. after INSERT, SELECT the row back. After crash recovery, SELECT again. If the row vanished, you were not in a committed transaction. Fetch sqlite.org/transactional.html rather than trusting a blog about fsync.
units.section: Relational Persistence: SQL & SQLite Internals › SQLite specifics

units.topic: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches
units.text: Math pack owns the formal definition of a function’s growth. This chapter is the engineering use: how many steps as input size n grows, so you pick a structure that will still return before the user leaves.
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.topic: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches
units.text: Definition. Big-O names an upper bound on growth, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. O(n) means “at most proportional to n, for large n.” it is not a timing in milliseconds. It is not a promise about n=3. Worst case unless you say average.
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.text: name: Constant; when you see it: Array index, hash-table hit (average), dict lookup
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.text: name: Logarithmic; when you see it: Binary search, balanced tree
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.text: name: Linear; when you see it: Scan a list, single pass
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.text: name: Linearithmic; when you see it: Good comparison sorts
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.text: name: Quadratic; when you see it: Nested loops over the same n
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.text: name: Exponential; when you see it: Naive subset / recursion without memory
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.topic: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches
units.text: Law. measure the input that actually grows. If you sort 20 config keys, O(n²) is noise. If you nest a linear scan inside a linear scan over a million rows, you will wait. Constants matter at small n; structure matters at large n. If you did not measure, you do not know the millisecond cost — call a profiler, not a model.
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches

units.text: get by key / index: O(1) index; insert: O(n) in the middle; amortised O(1) append; extra: Contiguous; good cache
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: get by key / index: O(n) scan; insert: O(1) at a known node; extra: Poor cache; rarely the default
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: get by key / index: Average O(1); insert: Average O(1); extra: Worst case O(n) if everything collides; no order
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: get by key / index: O(log n); insert: O(log n); extra: Ordered iteration
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: get by key / index: O(1) peek min/max; insert: O(log n) push/pop; extra: Not a search tree
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: get by key / index: O(log n); insert: O(log n); extra: Disk / SQLite indexes live here
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: get by key / index: O(1) at the end you chose; insert: O(1); extra: FIFO / LIFO
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: A graph is nodes plus edges. BFS/DFS are O(V+E) on an adjacency list if you mark visited. Binary search requires a sorted array; the sort is the precondition. Dijkstra on non-negative weights is the standard shortest-path tool; fetch a named algorithms text if you need the exact heap complexity for your variant. Do not quote a number you did not check.
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: You have n user ids and want “is this id in the set?” n times.
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: • List scan each time: n queries × n scan = O(n²) • Put ids in a hash set once O(n), then n lookups average O(1) each = O(n)
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: For n=10 both feel instant. For n=10^6 the nested scan is a bug. calc n*n if you want the comparison count; the Stacks does not invent a clock time.
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: Check. name n, name the structure, name the class. If you wrote a double for over the same array and n is unbounded, you owe a reason or a different structure. If you say O(1) and you walk the whole table, you lied.
units.section: Algorithmic Complexity in Practice: Big-O & CPU Caches › structures

units.text: Definition. an error is a named failure the caller can handle. It is not a printed stack that vanishes. It is not null with no comment.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › errors

units.text: is: In the spec: bad input, not found, conflict; example: 404, ValueError, unique-key fail
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › errors

units.text: is: A bug or an environment break; example: Null deref, disk full, upstream 500
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › errors

units.text: Law. expected errors stay structured (type, code, field). Unexpected errors fail closed: stop the operation, roll back the transaction, log with a correlation id, return 500 or crash the worker. Do not convert an unexpected error into an empty success.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › errors

units.text: Map errors at the boundary. Inside the core, use types. At HTTP, use RFC 9110 status. Do not leak stack traces to the public client.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › errors

units.text: Definition. a log is a time-ordered record of facts a human or a machine can grep later. It is not a debug print you will delete. It is not a second database of user content.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › logs

units.text: Each line should contain : time [UTC], level, correlation id, the operation, the outcome, and identifiers that are not secrets. One event per line. JSON logs are greppable if you keep the schema small.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › logs

units.text: Law. never log tokens, passwords, raw cards, session cookies, or private message bodies. Log the id of the object, not the secret that opens it. If you are unsure whether a field is a secret, it is a secret.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › logs

units.text: Levels : error = operator must look; warn = degraded; info = state change you would want in an incident; debug = off in production unless a named session turns it on.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › logs

units.text: Check. trigger a 500 in dev. The log line must name the request id and the function. The HTTP body must not contain the stack. The token used to call the API must not appear in the log file.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › logs

units.text: Definition. an operation is idempotent if doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once. RFC 9110 §9.2.2 defines this for HTTP methods. You also need it for your POST handlers, because networks retry.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › idempotence and retries

units.text: Timeout. a deadline, then stop. An unbounded wait is not patience; it is a leak of workers.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › idempotence and retries

units.text: Retry. only if the operation is idempotent or you have a dedupe key. Retrying a non-idempotent POST without a key is how you double-charge.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › idempotence and retries

units.text: Law. any effect that charges money, sends mail, or creates a unique real-world event must be keyed. The client sends an idempotency key. The server stores the key with the result. A second POST with the same key returns the first result and does not repeat the effect.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › idempotence and retries

units.text: • Client generates key = <uuid> • POST /charges with header Idempotency-Key: <key> and body { "amount": 10 } • Server INSERT the key first (unique constraint). If the insert loses a race, SELECT the stored result and return it • A retry with the same key does not create a second charge
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › idempotence and retries

units.text: GET, PUT, DELETE are already idempotent at the HTTP layer if you implemented them as RFC 9110 says. POST is not; you add the key.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › idempotence and retries

units.text: Check. send the same POST twice in a test. Assert one row, one side effect. If two rows appear, the handler is not idempotent. Fail closed. Unplug the network in the middle of the write. Does retry duplicate? if you do not know, you have not designed it.
units.section: Fault Tolerance: Error Envelopes, Structured Logs & Idempotence › idempotence and retries

units.text: Definition. a secret is a value that grants power: API token, private key, password, session signing key, webhook secret, cloud credential. If it is in a git object, it is in every clone of that history, forever until you rotate the secret and purge the object (purging hashes is hard; rotation is the real fix).
units.section: Cryptographic Secrets & Supply-Chain Hygiene

units.text: • Secrets live in the environment or in a restricted secret store, not in source. • .env files are local. They are listed in .gitignore. They are never git addEd. • Example files are env.example with empty or fake values. • If a secret was committed, rotate it now. Rewriting history without rotating leaves the old secret valid in every laptop that already fetched. • CI gets secrets from the host’s secret mechanism, not from a file in the repo. • Do not paste tokens into a model prompt. The prompt is not a vault. • Least privilege: the token that can only do this job.
units.section: Cryptographic Secrets & Supply-Chain Hygiene

units.text: GitHub documents secret scanning and removing sensitive data : https://docs.github.com/en — fetch the current page if you are in an incident. The Git book covers credential helpers; it does not make it legal to commit a token.
units.section: Cryptographic Secrets & Supply-Chain Hygiene

units.text: Supply chain. dependencies are code you did not write running in your process. Pin versions with a lockfile. Read the licence. A postinstall script is a program you just executed. Lockfiles exist so two installs match.
units.section: Cryptographic Secrets & Supply-Chain Hygiene

units.text: EasyLM is AGPL-3.0-or-later. Dependencies keep their own licences (model weights are not AGPL just because the app is). Say the split in the README. Do not launder a proprietary blob as “the app is free” without that split.
units.section: Cryptographic Secrets & Supply-Chain Hygiene

units.text: Missing env → fail closed (KeyError / explicit error), not a silent empty string that calls the API unsigned.
units.section: Cryptographic Secrets & Supply-Chain Hygiene

units.text: Grep the tree for sk-, BEGIN PRIVATE KEY, ghp_, AKIA. If you find a real one, rotate. Do not “just delete the file” in a new commit and call it done — the blob is still in history.
units.section: Cryptographic Secrets & Supply-Chain Hygiene

units.text: Check. git grep and git log -p --all -S 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY'. Empty is the passing test. A comment that says “do not commit secrets” is not a check.
units.section: Cryptographic Secrets & Supply-Chain Hygiene

units.topic: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment
units.text: Definition. shipping is moving a specific version of the program to a place users can run, with a way to roll back. For a front-end web app the usual shape is: source → build → static files → host that serves them over HTTPS.
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment

units.text: A build is a pure function from source + lockfile to artefacts. Given the same git commit and the same tool versions, you should get the same files (or a documented reason you do not).
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › build

units.text: • Install dependencies from a lockfile (package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, Cargo.lock) • Typecheck • Run tests (fail closed) • Compile/bundle TypeScript/JS/CSS to a dist/ of HTML, JS, CSS, assets • The server users hit is either that static dist/ or a small backend plus dist/
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › build

units.text: Vite (https://vite.dev/guide/) is one bundler used for this; the law is the pipeline, not the brand. TypeScript’s contract is the handbook at https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html. MDN documents the Web platform the bundle runs on: https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › build

units.text: Law. you ship the artefact, not your node_modules. You pin versions. An unpinned latest on the day you ship is a different program tomorrow. A git SHA is evidence of source; the live JS hash is evidence of what users run. They must match the build you meant.
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › build

units.text: Static hosting means : files on disk, HTTPS in front, index.html for the app shell, correct Content-Type, and a rule for client-side routes [usually “unknown path serves index.html” for a single-page app, except for real files].
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.text: why: HTTP scheme is a different origin; credentials leak on the wire
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.topic: Cache hashed assets forever; index.html short cache
units.text: why: Otherwise users keep a stale shell or re-download everything
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.text: why: JS served as text/plain will not run
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.text: why: Anything in dist/ is public. Public keys for a client API are not secrets; private keys are
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.topic: Source maps off or restricted in production
units.text: why: Maps are a gift to attackers if they include original source and you did not mean to publish it
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.text: why: You can point DNS or a release alias back
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.topic: Origin / CORS match the documented origins
units.text: why: A prefix regex that lets an attacker’s sibling host through is a hole
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.text: Rollback. keep the previous dist/ (or the previous container image tag). Shipping without a pointer to “last known good” is a one-way door.
units.section: Production Delivery: Static Packaging & Web Deployment › static host

units.text: CI. the pipeline is a test that runs on a clean machine. Install from lockfile, test, build. If CI is skippable, it is fail open. The README command and the CI command must be the same job.

units.text: Definition. a type is a name for a set of values and the operations that are legal on them. At the software-engineering layer, types are how you keep the spec from rotting: if the JSON field is a string id, the type says string, not “whatever.”

units.text: Law. the public surface is typed and small. Internals can be messy for a day; the surface cannot. If the function can return empty or a value, the type says so. If HTTP can return 404, the client type is a result, not a naked record.

units.topic: Systematic Debugging: The Scientific Method in Silicon
units.text: • name the failure in one sentence. • reproduce in one command or one request. If you cannot reproduce, you do not have a bug yet; you have a story. • smallest input that still fails. The smallest JSON that 500s is the spec of the bug. • name the layer: spec wrong, test wrong, code wrong, data wrong, environment wrong. Only one is the first cause. • read the error. status, exception type, log line with correlation id. If there is no log line, add one, do not add features. • bisect. git bisect on a failing test is faster than staring. Git records snapshots; use them. • check the RFC / language door if the fight is about HTTP, JSON, SQL, or git. Folklore loses. • arithmetic goes to calc.

units.text: classical chinese philosophical text comprising 81 chapters divided into book I the dao and book II the de.
traditional author of the tao te ching associated with spring and autumn and warring states classical period.
chapter 1 core axiom stating the dao that can be described or named in words is not the eternal absolute dao.
classical daoist principle of non-coercive non-contriving action moving in effortless alignment with natural systemic gradients.
symbol of original unconditioned simplicity and maximal entropy possessing unbounded potential before artificial specialization.
philosophical concept of primordial spontaneity and self-so naturalness existing without imposed external artifice.
cosmological principle that opposing complementary forces mutually generate, sustain, and define each other in dynamic equilibrium.
chapter 2 principle stating beauty and ugliness, difficult and easy, long and short, high and low define each other through contrast.
chapter 4 metaphor modeling dao as bottomless reservoir that is used without ever being exhausted or filled.
chapter 5 statement that heaven and earth are impartial treating ten thousand things like ceremonial straw dogs without favoritism.
shang shan ruo shui principle holding that highest excellence resembles water benefiting all things without contention and seeking low ground.
chapter 11 axiom demonstrating utility of wheel spokes, clay vessels, and rooms resides entirely in their hollow empty void.
chapter 16 doctrine stating attaining utmost emptiness and maintaining stillness allows ten thousand things to flourish and return to their root.
chapter 17 political axiom stating of highest rulers people barely know they exist, and when their task is done people say we did it ourselves.
chapter 22 paradox holding that what bends stays unbroken, what is bent becomes straight, and what is empty becomes full.
chapter 25 cosmological hierarchy stating humans follow earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows dao, and dao follows ziran.
chapter 33 distinction stating knowing others is ordinary intelligence, but knowing oneself is enlightened wisdom.
chapter 38 moral erosion stating when dao is lost virtue arises, when virtue is lost benevolence arises, when benevolence is lost righteousness arises, when righteousness is lost ritual arises.
Movement of dao is return: chapter 40 mechanical law stating returning is movement of dao and yielding is function of dao; ten thousand things are born from being, and being from non-being.
chapter 42 genesis stating dao generates one, one generates two, two generates three, and three generates ten thousand things.
paradoxical law stating softest substances in the world overcome hardest materials just as water erodes solid granite.
chapter 48 epistemic contrast stating pursuit of academic learning gains daily while pursuit of dao decreases daily until non-action is reached.
chapter 56 aphorism stating those who truly know do not speak, and those who speak incessantly do not know.
ruling principle advising that governing a large nation requires gentle restraint like cooking a delicate small fish without over-turning.
